slides.title: Earth's Blanket of Air
slides.kicker: Look up: the sky is a life-saving blanket
bullets: The atmosphere is a blanket of air surrounding the Earth, pulled down around it by gravity.
It is a mixture of gases in various proportions, vital for the survival of all living beings.
It shields us from the Sun's harmful radiation, including ultraviolet radiation.
slides.note: No air, no us. Imagine that for a second!

slides.title: Two Gases Rule the Air
slides.kicker: Nitrogen and oxygen make 99 per cent of air
bullets: Nitrogen and oxygen are the two primary and most abundant gases, essential to life on the Earth.
Nitrogen makes up 78 per cent and oxygen 21 per cent of the atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide, argon, helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone and hydrogen appear in lesser quantities.
slides.note: 78 plus 21 is 99. Air is basically nitrogen and oxygen.

slides.title: Vapour, Dust and Height
slides.kicker: The tiny parts of air do big jobs
bullets: Water vapour generally ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 per cent of the atmosphere, and the amount varies.
It plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation.
The atmosphere also carries tiny dust particles, and its composition varies with altitude.

right.title: Dust and altitude
items: composition changes as you go higher

slides.note: Chhoti cheezein, bada kaam.

slides.title: Why We Need This Blanket
slides.kicker: One shield, many superpowers
bullets: The atmosphere regulates the Earth's temperature by trapping some of the Sun's energy.
It prevents that energy from escaping back into space, keeping the planet comfortable for life.
It is a key component of weather and climate, influencing temperature, humidity and air pressure.
slides.note: LET'S RECALL asks how nitrogen helps plants. Revisit your Grade 8 chapter.

slides.title: Weather Is Today's Mood
slides.kicker: Will it rain today? That is weather
bullets: Weather refers to the hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere.
It can vary significantly from one day to the next.
Hot or humid weather may make one irritable, while pleasant or breezy weather makes one cheerful or even plans an outing.
slides.note: Plan the outing only after checking the sky, dost.

slides.title: Climate Is the Long Average
slides.kicker: Thirty years of weather, summed up
bullets: Climate refers to the average weather conditions of a place over a longer period of time.
It is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area.
This extended period is usually thirty years or more.

items: Average over thirty years or more

slides.note: Weather is a mood, climate is a personality.

slides.title: Weather vs Climate
slides.kicker: Same sky, two time scales
bullets: Weather is about right now: today's rain, sunshine or breeze where you live.
Climate describes a large area over an extended period, so it changes slowly.
Use weather for today's plans and climate to describe a region's long-term pattern.
slides.note: Exam favourite. Keep both definitions ready.

slides.title: Five Elements in Action
slides.kicker: What actually shapes weather and climate
bullets: The major elements are temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure.
These elements of the atmosphere impact human life on the Earth.
Each element can change under varying conditions.
slides.note: Memorise this list of five first.

slides.title: Insolation Sets Temperature
slides.kicker: The Sun writes the temperature map
bullets: Insolation is the incoming solar energy from the Sun that is intercepted by the Earth.
The amount of insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles, where sunlight arrives at a low angle.
Hence the temperature decreases from the equator towards the poles.
Temperature also varies between day and night and across seasons, since summers are hotter than winters.

items: Sun's rays strike the equator directly
Rays slant at low angles near the poles

slides.note: Insolation means INcoming SOLar energy, intercepted by Earth.

slides.title: Three Temperature Zones
slides.kicker: Torrid, Temperate and Frigid belts
bullets: Sunlight strikes most directly at the equator, so the Torrid Zone around it is the hottest belt.
The Temperate Zones lie between the Tropics at 23.5 degrees and the Circles at 66.5 degrees.
The Frigid Zones lie beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles, where sunlight comes in at a low angle.
slides.note: 23.5 degrees means 23 and a half degrees north or south.

slides.title: Humidity: Air Holding Water
slides.kicker: Gheelesh weather? Thank humidity
bullets: Water evaporating from land and different water bodies becomes water vapour in the air.
Humidity is the presence of water vapour in the air, creating moisture.
As air gets warmer, its capacity to hold water vapour increases, so humidity levels rise.
On such days clothes take longer to dry and sweat evaporates slowly, leaving us uncomfortable.

items: Water evaporates from land and seas

slides.note: Sweat refuses to dry on a muggy day.

slides.title: Precipitation: Air Lets Go
slides.kicker: Drizzle to hail, water falls home
bullets: Precipitation occurs when part of the atmosphere becomes saturated with water vapour.
The vapour condenses and falls on the Earth due to gravity as drizzle, rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Rain is the most common form of precipitation and lowers the temperature of a place.
Prevailing winds, mountains and seasons affect precipitation, and most groundwater comes from rainwater.
slides.note: A long absence of rainfall results in a dry climate.

slides.title: Air Has Weight: Pressure
slides.kicker: An invisible ocean pushes on you
bullets: The pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface is called air pressure.
Air pressure is one of the five major elements, and the book explores what happens as we go higher in the atmosphere.
The chapter asks you to think: why do you not feel the pressure of the atmosphere?
slides.note: Question 4 of the chapter wants your answer here.

slides.title: India: Tropical Monsoon Land
slides.kicker: One word explains our skies: monsoon
bullets: The climate of India can be broadly classified as tropical monsoon.
The Indian Meteorological Department, the IMD, has recognised four distinct seasons in India.
The Himalayan states, being more temperate, also experience two additional seasons, autumn and spring.
slides.note: IMD means Indian Meteorological Department.

slides.title: Winter and Summer Compared
slides.kicker: From 10 degrees to 40 degrees
bullets: Winter generally lasts from December to early April, and December and January are the coldest months.
The north-west averages around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius, rising towards the equator to 20 to 25 in the south-east.
Summer or pre-monsoon spans April to June, up to July in north-western India, with most inland areas at 32 to 40 degrees.
April is the hottest month in western and southern regions, while May is hottest in northern regions.

right.title: Summer
items: April to June, or July in the north-west
Hottest: April in south and west

slides.note: All temperatures here are in degrees Celsius.

slides.title: The Advancing Monsoon
slides.kicker: June se September: rain takes over
bullets: The monsoon or rainy season, called the advancing monsoon, generally spans June to September.
It is dominated by the humid south-west summer monsoon, which sweeps across the country in late May or early June.
Monsoon rain begins to recede from north India at the beginning of October.
South India typically receives more rainfall during this time.

items: Late May or early June: monsoon arrives
June to September: rains sweep the country
Early October: rain recedes from north India

slides.note: The four main seasons is a guaranteed exam question.

slides.title: Retreating Monsoon Months
slides.kicker: Clear October skies in the north-west
bullets: The post-monsoon or retreating monsoon season lasts from October to December.
In north-western India, October and November are usually cloudless.
The chapter also asks you to distinguish the south-west monsoon from the north-east monsoon.
slides.note: Practise comparing the two monsoons in your answer.

slides.title: Six Ritus of Bhaarata
slides.kicker: The traditional calendar sings six seasons
bullets: Traditionally, India experiences six seasons, each about two months long.
They are based on the astronomical division of the 12 months into six parts.
Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira map onto the months of the Indian calendar.
For example, Varsha is Shravana-Bhadrapada, roughly July and August, and durations vary across the country.
slides.note: Hindustani ragas are linked to seasons. Ask your elders.

slides.title: The Chapter's Question Bank
slides.kicker: Time to test your atmosphere knowledge
bullets: The book asks for a pie diagram of the atmosphere's composition and a labelled diagram of its structure.
You must name the four main seasons of India and distinguish the troposphere from the stratosphere.
Other questions ask why we do not feel atmospheric pressure, which layer aeroplanes fly in, and why.
slides.note: Attempt each one before peeking at any answer.

slides.title: Graphing Ten Stations
slides.kicker: Turn a data table into climate pictures
bullets: Table 3.3 shows average monthly temperatures and rainfall amounts for 10 representative stations.
The do-it-yourself activity converts these figures into temperature and rainfall graphs.
The graphs help you grasp similarities and differences in our diverse climatic conditions at a glance.
slides.note: One sample graph is already prepared in the book.

slides.title: Ten Stations, Many Climates
slides.kicker: From Leh to Thiruvananthapuram
bullets: The stations range from Thiruvananthapuram at 8 degrees 29 minutes N to Leh at 34 degrees N.
Altitudes vary too, from Kolkata at 6 metres to Shillong high at 1461 metres, with Bengaluru at 909 metres.
Activity 7.1 asks you to re-arrange the 10 stations according to their distance from the equator.
slides.note: Same latitude, different altitude, different climate.

slides.title: Climate Detective Questions
slides.kicker: Why more rain here and less there?
bullets: The book asks why Shillong experiences more rainfall than Kolkata, and why Delhi receives more rainfall than Jodhpur.
You must find two stations with the most extreme climate and two influenced by retreating monsoons.
Another task is to spot the two hottest stations in February and again in June, then draw broad generalisations.
slides.note: Our diverse climatic conditions are the real answer.

flashcards.front: What is the atmosphere?
flashcards.back: A blanket of air surrounding the Earth, held by gravity, made of a mixture of gases vital for all living beings.

flashcards.front: Which two gases are most abundant in air?
flashcards.back: Nitrogen (78 per cent) and oxygen (21 per cent), the two primary gases essential to life on the Earth.

flashcards.front: What per cent of air is water vapour?
flashcards.back: Generally 0.1 to 0.4 per cent, though it varies; it plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation.

flashcards.front: Name four gases found in lesser quantities in air.
flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide, argon, helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone and hydrogen, in smaller quantities.

flashcards.front: What keeps the atmosphere wrapped around Earth?
flashcards.back: Gravity. Earth's gravity pulls the blanket of air down around the planet.

flashcards.front: Define weather.
flashcards.back: The hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere, which can vary significantly day to day.

flashcards.front: Define climate.
flashcards.back: The average weather conditions of a place over a long period, usually thirty years or more.

flashcards.front: How can weather change your mood?
flashcards.back: Hot or humid weather may make one irritable, while pleasant or breezy weather makes one cheerful or plan an outing.

flashcards.front: Name the five major elements of weather and climate.
flashcards.back: Temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure.

flashcards.front: What is insolation?
flashcards.back: The incoming solar energy from the Sun that is intercepted by the Earth.

flashcards.front: Why is it cooler near the poles than at the equator?
flashcards.back: Insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles, so temperature decreases the same way.

flashcards.front: Name the three temperature zones of the Earth.
flashcards.back: The Torrid Zone, the Temperate Zones and the Frigid Zones, shown between 23.5 and 66.5 degree markers.

flashcards.front: Define humidity.
flashcards.back: The presence of water vapour in the air, creating moisture; warmer air can hold more water vapour.

flashcards.front: List the forms of precipitation named in the book.
flashcards.back: Drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail. Rain is the most common form.

flashcards.front: Which three main factors affect precipitation?
flashcards.back: Prevailing winds, mountains and seasons.

flashcards.front: What is air pressure?
flashcards.back: The pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface.

flashcards.front: Which four seasons does the IMD recognise in India?
flashcards.back: Winter, summer or pre-monsoon, monsoon or advancing monsoon, and post-monsoon or retreating monsoon.

flashcards.front: When are the coldest months in India?
flashcards.back: December and January, with north-west averages around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius.

flashcards.front: Name the six traditional Indian seasons (Rtu).
flashcards.back: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira, each about two months long.

flashcards.front: Which extra seasons do the Himalayan states enjoy?
flashcards.back: Autumn and spring, because these states are more temperate.

flashcards.front: Who recorded rainfall measurements long ago in India?
flashcards.back: Kautilya's Arthashastra records scientific rainfall measurements used practically to manage the country.

flashcards.front: What data does Table 3.3 provide?
flashcards.back: Average monthly temperatures and rainfall for 10 representative stations, with annual rainfall totals.

flashcards.front: Which two rain comparisons does the book ask about?
flashcards.back: Why Shillong gets more rainfall than Kolkata, and why Delhi receives more rainfall than Jodhpur.

flashcards.front: What should the station graphs help you see?
flashcards.back: Broad similarities and differences in our diverse climatic conditions, at a glance.

quiz.q: Which gas makes up about 78 per cent of the atmosphere?
quiz.why: The composition pie diagram shows nitrogen at 78 per cent.

quiz.q: Which pair names the two primary and most abundant gases in air?
quiz.why: The book calls nitrogen and oxygen the two primary gases essential to life.

quiz.q: What is the share of argon in the atmosphere?
quiz.why: The pie diagram lists argon at 0.93 per cent, far more than carbon dioxide's 0.04.

quiz.q: Which statement about water vapour in the atmosphere is correct?
options: It stays fixed at 5 per cent
It ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 per cent
It is present only in summer
It never varies from place to place
quiz.why: Water vapour generally ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 per cent and its amount varies.

quiz.q: Besides gases, what else does the atmosphere consist of?
options: Water vapour and tiny dust particles
quiz.why: The atmosphere also consists of water vapour and tiny dust particles.

quiz.q: Weather refers to which conditions of the atmosphere?
quiz.why: Weather is defined as the hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Climate is usually measured over about how long a period?
quiz.why: Climate averages weather over an extended period, usually thirty years or more.

quiz.q: Which sentence describes climate, not weather?
options: Last week was hotter than this week
This place gets heavy rain in most years
The wind feels breezy right now
quiz.why: Climate is the sum total of weather conditions over a large area for an extended period.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a major element of weather and climate?
quiz.why: The major elements are temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure.

quiz.q: Insolation is best defined as the incoming solar energy that is —
options: radiated by the Earth at night
quiz.why: The book defines insolation as incoming solar energy from the Sun intercepted by the Earth.

quiz.q: Why does temperature decrease from the equator towards the poles?
quiz.why: Insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles, hence temperature falls.

quiz.q: The most common form of precipitation is —
quiz.why: Rain is the most common form and it lowers the temperature of a place.

quiz.q: On a very humid day you feel uncomfortable because —
quiz.why: With high humidity, sweat evaporates slowly and clothes take longer to dry.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes how precipitation occurs?
options: Air saturates, vapour condenses, gravity pulls it down
Vapour freezes, wind lifts, clouds dissolve
Rain falls first, then air saturates
Gravity condenses air, wind saturates water
quiz.why: Saturated water vapour condenses and precipitates, falling on the Earth due to gravity.

quiz.q: How many distinct seasons does the IMD recognise in India?
quiz.why: The Indian Meteorological Department has recognised four distinct seasons.

quiz.q: The coldest months of the year in India are —
quiz.why: December and January are coldest, with the north-west averaging 10 to 15 degrees Celsius.

quiz.q: The advancing monsoon generally spans which months?
quiz.why: The monsoon or rainy season generally spans June to September.

quiz.q: In which regions is April the hottest month of summer?
quiz.why: April is hottest in the west and south, while May is hottest in northern regions.

quiz.q: In post-monsoon October and November, north-western India is usually —
quiz.why: The book says north-western India is usually cloudless in October and November.

quiz.q: Which Rtu pairs with the Indian calendar months Shravana-Bhadrapada?
quiz.why: Varsha spans Shravana-Bhadrapada, roughly July and August in the Gregorian calendar.

quiz.q: Hindustani classical music associates seasons with —
quiz.why: The book says certain ragas are connected to specific seasons.

quiz.q: Table 3.3 gives temperature and rainfall data for how many stations?
quiz.why: Table 3.3 lists 10 representative stations across India.

quiz.q: Which station in Table 3.3 lies farthest from the equator?
quiz.why: Leh at 34 degrees N has the highest latitude, so it is farthest from the equator.

quiz.q: Which of these stations is closest to the equator?
quiz.why: Thiruvananthapuram's latitude of 8 degrees 29 minutes N is the lowest in the table.

quiz.q: Activity 7.1 asks you to re-arrange the ten stations by —
quiz.why: Activity 7.1 says to arrange the stations according to their distance from the equator.

examples.title: Check the Air's Pie Chart
examples.problem: Use the composition diagram of the atmosphere to verify that the listed gases add up to 100 per cent, and find how much of the air is nitrogen and oxygen together.
steps: List the shares from the diagram: nitrogen 78, oxygen 21, argon 0.93, carbon dioxide 0.04, others 0.03.
Add them in order: 78 plus 21 gives 99, then 99 plus 0.93 gives 99.93, then 99.93 plus 0.04 gives 99.97, and 99.97 plus 0.03 gives 100.
So the listed gases account for the entire atmosphere.
The trace gases beyond nitrogen and oxygen together make only about 1 per cent of the air.
examples.answer: Nitrogen plus oxygen make 99 per cent of the atmosphere, and all listed shares add up to exactly 100 per cent.

examples.title: Weather or Climate? Decide
examples.problem: Classify each observation as weather or climate: a) the sky is cloudy this morning, b) this region receives most of its rain in the monsoon months over the decades, c) yesterday was humid and everyone felt irritable, d) the average conditions of a place over thirty years.
steps: Ask two questions: is it right now or day-to-day, and does it cover a large area over an extended period?
a) This morning's clouds are hour-to-hour conditions, so it is weather.
b) A rainfall pattern over decades for a large area is climate.
c) Yesterday's humidity is a day-to-day condition, so it is weather.
d) A thirty-year average is exactly the book's definition of climate.
examples.answer: a is weather, b is climate, c is weather, d is climate. The time scale and area size decide the label.

examples.title: Order the Stations by Latitude
examples.problem: Using Table 3.3, arrange Thiruvananthapuram (8 degrees 29 minutes N), Chennai (13 degrees 4 minutes N), Shillong (24 degrees 34 minutes N) and Delhi (29 degrees N) from closest to farthest from the equator.
steps: Convert each latitude to plain degrees: 8 degrees 29 minutes is about 8.5, 13 degrees 4 minutes is about 13.1, 24 degrees 34 minutes is about 24.6, and Delhi is 29.
Remember the rule: the smaller the latitude, the closer the station sits to the equator.
Order the values from smallest to largest: 8.5, then 13.1, then 24.6, then 29.
Match each value back to its station from Table 3.3.
examples.answer: Closest to farthest from the equator: Thiruvananthapuram, Chennai, Shillong, Delhi.

examples.title: Who Has the Hotter Month?
examples.problem: Aditi in northern India says May is the hottest month, while her cousin in southern India says April is. Who is right, and what summer temperatures do most inland places record?
steps: Check the book's facts for the summer or pre-monsoon season, which spans April to June.
In western and southern regions, the hottest month is April.
In northern regions, the hottest month is May.
The average temperature across most of inland India in this season ranges from 32 to 40 degrees Celsius.
examples.answer: Both are right in their own regions: April in the south and west, May in the north, with inland summer averages of 32 to 40 degrees Celsius.
